title: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a dimensionality-reduction technique that transforms a set of correlated variables into a smaller set of uncorrelated variables called principal components. Each principal component is a linear combination of the original features, and the components are ordered so that the first captures the most variance in the data, the second captures the next most, and so on. Like clustering, PCA is unsupervised. It does not use any outcome or label. It reveals which combinations of features carry the most information and how the observations relate to one another in a lower-dimensional space.
At the heart of PCA lies the covariance (or correlation) matrix of the standardized data. This matrix summarizes how each pair of variables varies together. An eigenvector of this matrix is a direction in feature space that is unchanged (up to scaling) when the covariance matrix is applied to it. In PCA terms, eigenvectors are the directions of the principal components. The corresponding eigenvalue measures how much variance of the data lies along that direction. The largest eigenvalue corresponds to the first principal component (PC1), the second largest to PC2, and so on. Because eigenvectors are orthogonal (perpendicular), the principal components are uncorrelated with each other, where each captures a distinct dimension of variation.
Mathematically, PCA solves:
\[
\Sigma v_i = \lambda_i v_i
\]
where \(\Sigma\) is the covariance matrix, \(v_i\) is the \(i\)-th eigenvector, and \(\lambda_i\) is its eigenvalue. The loading of each original variable on a component is given by the corresponding entry of the eigenvector.



In high dimensions, structure is hidden. PCA reveals it.





PCA finds the directions of maximum variance.


Dimensionality reduction means replacing a large set of features with a smaller set that retains most of the information. In PCA, we keep the first \(k\) principal components, which together explain most of the total variance. This reduces the number of dimensions without discarding the underlying signal.
High-dimensional data is difficult to work with for several reasons:

Visualization is impossible beyond three dimensions. PCA lets us project data onto two or three axes we can actually plot.
Distance calculations become unreliable. In high dimensions, all points tend to be roughly equidistant.
Models overfit more easily. More features than observations lead to unstable estimates. Reducing dimensions can improve generalization.
Collinearity is common. In our dataset, Revenue, Net Income, and Total Assets are strongly correlated. PCA collapses these into a single component that captures “size,” removing redundancy.
Noise accumulates. With many features, noise can dominate the signal.

In this section, we do the following:

Reduce our 17 financial and market features into a small number of components that retain most of the variance.
Visualize the 40 companies in a two-dimensional PCA space to see whether sectors separate naturally.
Interpret the components by examining their loadings

title: Principal Component Analysis
text:
Code
The full R code for the PCA is embedded below.


Code
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(factoextra)
library(FactoMineR)

# --- 1. Load and standardize ---
fin    <- read_csv("data/clean/company_financials_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
market <- read_csv("data/clean/market_data_clean.csv",        show_col_types = FALSE)
merged <- inner_join(fin, market, by = c("ticker", "company", "sector"))

pca_vars <- c(
  "Revenue","NetIncome","TotalAssets","TotalLiabilities","TotalEquity",
  "LongTermDebt","OperatingIncome","CashFromOperations",
  "ROA","ROE","Debt_to_Equity","Profit_Margin",
  "latest_price","avg_volume","total_return","volatility","beta"
)

pca_df  <- merged %>% select(ticker, all_of(pca_vars)) %>% na.omit()
pca_ids <- pca_df$ticker
X       <- scale(pca_df %>% select(-ticker))

# --- 2. Run PCA ---
pca_res <- prcomp(X, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)  # X is already standardized

# Eigenvalues and variance explained
eig_vals <- pca_res$sdev^2
var_exp  <- eig_vals / sum(eig_vals)
cum_var  <- cumsum(var_exp)

# Loadings (variable contributions)
loadings <- pca_res$rotation

# Scores (company coordinates)
scores <- as.data.frame(pca_res$x)
scores$ticker <- pca_ids

                geom.ind = "point",
                col.ind = merged$sector,
                palette = "jco",

                repel = TRUE,
                title = "PCA Biplot (Companies Colored by Sector)") +

PCA Biplot: Companies and Variables




Interpretation: - Technology and Healthcare on the high-profitability side. - Utilities and Energy on the high-leverage, low-profitability side. - Financials forming a distinct cluster due to their unusual balance sheets (large Total Liabilities, low ROA). - Consumer Staples somewhere in the middle, near the origin.

title: Understanding Financial Performance Through Machine Learning
text:
In May 2026, two of the world’s most recognizable companies reported results that could not have been more different. Nike announced major declines in its financial performance, while Microsoft reported a significant increase in net income.1 2 Both firms are large, well-managed, and globally recognized—yet their outcomes diverged sharply. This contrast is not unusual. It reflects a deeper truth about corporate finance: financial performance can varies greatly across companies, and understanding why remains one of the most important questions for investors, analysts, and policymakers.



A company’s performance does not exist in isolation. It is shaped by its industry, its size, its capital structure, and the broader economic environment in which it operates. A technology firm like Microsoft and a consumer-facing company like Nike face fundamentally different cost structures, growth trajectories, and risk profiles. Understanding the factors associated with financial performance can therefore provide a broader understanding of why some publicly traded companies outperform others, and what that means for the economy as a whole.



The increasing availability of financial and economic data has made it possible to examine corporate performance from a much wider perspective than before. Publicly traded companies now generate vast amounts of information through financial statements, regulatory filings, market activity, and other reporting channels. Combined with macroeconomic indicators such as interest rates, inflation, and GDP growth, this data creates new opportunities for systematic analysis.
Prior research has already begun to identify key drivers. Sujith et al. (2022) show that core financial inputs such as revenue and EBITDA have a direct effect on net profit, and they argue that a structured evaluation framework provides deeper insights than conventional, single-metric analysis. Ahmad et al. (2023) found that industry variation, firm size, technology use, and environmental uncertainty are significantly related to how well firms perform.



Traditional financial analysis often relies on a relatively small number of indicators examined directly. While these approaches remain valuable, they struggle to capture the complex, multidimensional relationships that emerge when many factors interact simultaneously. This creates an opportunity to use data-driven and machine learning approaches that can examine patterns across company characteristics, market conditions, and economic environments at once. These findings motivate this project’s broader investigation of the drivers of financial performance across publicly traded companies.




This project first explores whether the 40 companies in the dataset fall into groups based on their financial and market characteristics. Imagine sorting a collection of towels without knowing what any of them show. As one looks through them, one might notice they fit in different color categories, textures, material, and designs. Clustering works in a similar way by allowing patterns to emerge from the data without deciding on the groups beforehand. Another method the project uses is Principal Component Analysis (PCA). Imagine trying to describe a company using dozens of different financial measurements. Looking at every measurement individually can make it difficult to see the bigger picture, especially when several measurements tell us similar things. For example, a company with high revenue may also have substantial total assets, meaning that some of the information overlaps. PCA helps address this problem by combining related information into a smaller number of summary measures while preserving as much of the important variation in the data as possible.



This project explores the following questions, organized around four themes:
Company Characteristics and Performance

Which company characteristics are most strongly associated with financial performance?
How does company size relate to financial performance?
How is a company’s level of debt associated with its financial performance?
Is profitability associated with other measures of financial performance?

Industry and Sector Differences

How does financial performance differ across industries and sectors?

Macroeconomic Conditions

How are interest rates associated with corporate financial performance?
How does inflation relate to the financial performance of publicly traded companies?

Data-Driven Exploration

Do companies with similar financial characteristics exhibit similar levels of performance?
Are there distinct groups of publicly traded companies with different financial profiles?
Which combination of company, market, and economic characteristics provides the strongest explanation of differences in financial performance?

title: Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
The primary dataset comes from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) EDGAR system, accessed through the CompanyFacts API. This API fetches standardized XBRL financial-statement data for publicly traded companies and requires no API key. 40 large companies across eight sectors were selected to ensure diversity in size, industry, and capital structure.
Additional data sources like macroeconomic indicators and market data are introduced later on this page.



The SEC dataset provides the fundamental measures of performance: profitability, leverage, and balance-sheet composition. Python was used to connect to the API. The script performs the following steps:

Fetch the official company ticker mapping from company_tickers.json.
Select a list of 40 tickers spanning eight sectors.
For each company, call the CompanyFacts endpoint:
https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK{cik}.json
Extract key US-GAAP financial metrics from the latest 10-K filing.
Compute derived ratios (ROA, ROE, Debt-to-Equity, Profit Margin).
Save both raw and clean CSV files.

API endpoint example:
https://data.sec.gov/api/xbrl/companyfacts/CIK0000320193.json
(where 0000320193 is the CIK for Apple Inc.)
See the full Python code: code/company_financials.py



The raw data—stored in company_financials_raw.csv—is exactly what the SEC API returned. It contains the foundational financial metrics for each company’s most recent fiscal year (10-K filing), but it also contains gaps: Microsoft’s Total Liabilities, Meta’s Long-Term Debt, and several other fields show NA. This is common in raw financial data, since companies do not always report every standardized US-GAAP tag, and they may structure debt differently. Sector classification and derived ratios are also absent at this stage.
The following cleaning and transformation steps were performed in Python:

Impute missing values using the sector median, ensuring completeness without discarding entire rows.
Convert all numeric columns to float.
Compute three key ratios used throughout the analysis:

ROA (Return on Assets) = Net Income ÷ Total Assets
ROE (Return on Equity) = Net Income ÷ Total Equity
Debt-to-Equity = Long-Term Debt ÷ Total Equity

Add a sector column derived from ticker (manual mapping).

The result is company_financials_clean.csv—a structured, complete dataset ready for analysis.
The first ten rows of both versions appear below.

title: Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Data Source & Collection
Market data was obtained from Yahoo Finance using the Python library yfinance. Daily OHLCV data was collected for the same 40 companies from 2023-01-01 to present, and the following five features were computed for each company:

Latest Price — most recent closing price in the sample period.
Avg Volume — mean daily trading volume (a liquidity proxy).
Total Return — cumulative percentage price change from the first to the last day.
Volatility — annualized standard deviation of daily returns (std × √252); higher values indicate higher risk.
Beta — sensitivity of the stock’s returns to the S&P 500. Beta > 1 means the stock moves more than the market; Beta < 1 means less.

The full Python script is available here: code/market_data.py.
The raw market data is stored in market_data_raw.csv. Each row represents one trading day with the standard OHLCV fields. Although the sample appears clean (no missing values), the raw data is far too granular for cross-company analysis. It is therefore summarized into company-level risk metrics, stored in market_data_clean.csv. Each row in the clean file represents one publicly traded company, with five market-derived features to be merged with the financial dataset.
Previews of both are shown below.

Raw Market Data Preview



Raw market data preview




Clean Market Data Preview



Clean market data preview


These metrics will be merged with the financial dataset to explore the relationship between market risk and financial performance.

title: Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Summary Statistics



Summary statistics


The summary statistics reveal two consistent patterns: extreme skew and wide dispersion.

Revenue spans from $1.5 billion to $648 billion, with a mean ($97.6B) far above the median ($59.8B)—a clear sign of right-skew driven by Walmart ($648B) and Apple ($215B).
Net Income ranges from −$2.2 billion (a net loss) to $73.8 billion (Alphabet). The mean again exceeds the median, confirming skew.
Total Assets range from $12.8 billion to nearly $3.9 trillion (JPMorgan Chase), with a standard deviation of $808 billion—the widest spread in the dataset. This reflects the enormous differences in balance-sheet size across sectors, from banks to technology to consumer staples.



Code
ggplot(fin, aes(x = Revenue / 1e9)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 12, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(x = "Revenue (Billions USD)", y = "Number of Companies",
       title = "Distribution of Revenue Across 40 Companies") +
  theme_minimal()





Distribution of Revenue Across 40 Companies






Code
fin %>%
  arrange(ROA) %>%
  mutate(ticker = factor(ticker, levels = ticker)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ticker, y = ROA)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(fin$ROA, na.rm = TRUE),
             color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Return on Assets (ROA)",
       title = "ROA by Company (Ordered)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7))





ROA by Company (40 Tickers)




ROA averages 0.068 (6.8%) with a median of 0.056, ranging from −0.021 to 0.267. The negative minimum again signals at least one unprofitable company. Nvidia’s ROA of 0.267 is the strongest in the sample.


Code
fin %>%
  arrange(ROE) %>%
  mutate(ticker = factor(ticker, levels = ticker)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ticker, y = ROE, fill = sector)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Return on Equity (ROE)",
       title = "ROE by Company (Ordered)",
       fill = "Sector") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7))





ROE by Company (Ordered, 40 Tickers)




ROE has the widest relative spread of any variable (SD = 1.901), ranging from −1.411 to 11.960. UPS shows the maximum ROE (≈ 11.96)—but this is not a sign of exceptional profitability. It reflects an extremely small equity base, not large profits. The same pattern appears for AbbVie (ROE ≈ 1.46, Debt-to-Equity ≈ 19.4). This is exactly why ROE must be interpreted alongside leverage and equity size, and why ROA is a more reliable measure of operating performance.


Code
fin %>%
  arrange(Debt_to_Equity) %>%
  mutate(ticker = factor(ticker, levels = ticker)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ticker, y = Debt_to_Equity, fill = sector)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Debt-to-Equity",
       title = "Debt-to-Equity by Company (Ordered)",
       fill = "Sector") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, size = 7))





Debt-to-Equity by Company (Ordered, 40 Tickers)




Debt-to-Equity shows a striking outlier: a maximum of 30.602 and a minimum of −13.722. Negative values occur when total equity itself is negative, which happens when accumulated losses or buybacks exceed contributed capital.

title: Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Distribution of ROA by Sector


Code
fin %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(sector, ROA, FUN = median), y = ROA, fill = sector)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Sector", y = "Return on Assets", title = "ROA Distribution by Sector") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")





Return on Assets by Sector




This boxplot shows how ROA distributes across the eight sectors. Three patterns stand out.
Sector matters. Median ROA is highest in Technology and Healthcare, and lowest in Utilities and Energy. The difference reflects asset intensity: tech and healthcare firms rely more on intellectual property and less on heavy physical assets, whereas utilities and energy require massive capital investment in infrastructure.
Within-sector variation is large. The Technology sector alone spans a wide interquartile range—from Nvidia (ROA ≈ 0.267) to firms with much lower profitability. This shows sector alone does not fully explain performance.
Financials behave differently. Banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America sit at low ROA (median ≈ 0.013–0.015), because their asset bases are enormous relative to profits. ROA is simply not the primary performance metric for banks.
In short, ROA is strongly associated with sector, but the within-sector spread suggests other factors like leverage, efficiency, market conditions are at play.

title: Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Revenue vs. Net Income


Code
signed_sqrt <- trans_new("signed_sqrt",
  transform = function(x) sign(x) * sqrt(abs(x)),
  inverse = function(x) sign(x) * x^2,
  domain = c(-Inf, Inf)
)

fin %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Revenue, y = NetIncome, color = sector)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, position = position_jitter(width = 0.02, height = 0.02)) +
  scale_x_continuous(trans = signed_sqrt, labels = dollar_format(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "B")) +
  scale_y_continuous(trans = signed_sqrt, labels = dollar_format(scale = 1e-9, suffix = "B")) +
  labs(x = "Revenue (Signed Sqrt Scale, Billions)", y = "Net Income (Signed Sqrt Scale, Billions)", title = "Revenue vs. Net Income") +
  theme_minimal()





Revenue vs Net Income (signed square root scale)




This scatterplot shows the relationship between Revenue and Net Income for all 40 companies, colored by sector. Because both variables are highly skewed and include negative values, a signed square root transformation compresses large values while preserving the sign.
Higher revenue generally corresponds to higher net income, but the relationship is far from tight, and the scatter tells the real story. Consider two firms at opposite ends of the spectrum:

Walmart: Revenue ≈ $648B, Net Income ≈ $15.5B (Profit Margin ≈ 2.4%).
Nvidia: Revenue ≈ $60.9B, Net Income ≈ $29.8B (Profit Margin ≈ 48.9%).

Nvidia earns nearly twice Walmart’s net income on one-tenth of the revenue. Revenue size does not determine profitability. Business model and sector strongly shape how much of each revenue dollar survives to the bottom line. Technology and Healthcare firms cluster in the upper-middle region (high net income relative to revenue), while Energy and Utilities cluster lower.
While revenue is positively associated with net income, the wide dispersion justifies including profitability ratios (ROA, ROE, Profit Margin) as complementary performance measures.

title: Data Preparation and Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Merging with Financial Data
The market metrics are now merged with the financial dataset for joint analysis.

Volatility vs. ROA


Code
merged %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = volatility, y = ROA, color = sector)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Annualized Volatility", y = "Return on Assets", title = "Volatility vs. ROA") +
  theme_minimal()





Volatility vs. Return on Assets




This scatterplot relates annualized market volatility to Return on Assets, colored by sector. It directly addresses the guiding question: Does greater market volatility tend to be associated with differences in company financial performance?
The points are widely scattered and show no clear upward or downward trend. Volatility alone is a poor predictor of accounting profitability. Sector clustering is still visible with Technology firms at the lower-volatility, higher-ROA region, while Utilities and Financials sit in the lower-volatility, lower-ROA region. But this may simply reflect the fact that volatility and ROA both depend on sector.
Nvidia and Tesla stand out with volatility > 0.48 and beta > 2.0. Nvidia also has a high ROA (≈ 0.267), while Tesla’s is more modest (≈ 0.123). High market risk can accompany strong profitability, but it doesn’t guarantee it.


Beta vs. ROA


Code
merged %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = beta, y = ROA, color = sector)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Beta", y = "Return on Assets", title = "Beta vs. ROA") +
  theme_minimal()





Beta vs. Return on Assets




Replacing volatility with Beta (that is, the stock’s sensitivity to the overall market) produces a similar picture. As with volatility, there is no strong monotonic relationship between market risk and ROA. Defensive, low-beta firms (Walmart at 0.40, AbbVie at 0.25) span a range of ROA values, and high-beta firms (Tesla at 2.30, Nvidia at 2.12) span a different range. Neither risk measure is a clean predictor of profitability on its own.


Total Return by Sector


Code
merged %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(sector, total_return, FUN = median), y = total_return, fill = sector)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = "Sector", y = "Total Return", title = "Total Return Distribution by Sector") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")





Total Return by Sector




This boxplot shows the distribution of total return (cumulative price change from 2023-01-01 to the present) for each sector, sorted by median return.
Sector dominates. Technology and Communication Services lead by a wide margin, driven by Nvidia (~1,430%), Meta (~424%), and Alphabet (~283%). Consumer Staples and Healthcare lag, with median returns of roughly 80–130%. This is consistent with the risk/return profile observed earlier.
This reinforces the need to treat sector as a grouping variable in later ML models rather than pooling all companies together.


Correlation Matrix
Pairwise correlations reveal which features are strongly related and which may be redundant.


Code
library(reshape2)
library(ggplot2)

corr_vars <- merged %>%
  select(Revenue, NetIncome, TotalAssets, ROA, ROE,
         Debt_to_Equity, Profit_Margin, volatility, beta, total_return)

corr_mat <- cor(corr_vars, use = "complete.obs")
melted <- melt(corr_mat)

ggplot(melted, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2, fill = value)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(value, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "firebrick", mid = "white", high = "steelblue",
                       midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Correlation Matrix", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))





Correlation Matrix of Financial and Market Variables




Four patterns emerge:

Size variables cluster tightly. Revenue, Net Income, and Total Assets are strongly positively correlated: larger firms are larger on every dimension. This creates multicollinearity, which matters for linear models.
Profitability ratios cluster moderately. ROA, ROE, and Profit Margin are positively correlated with each other, but not perfectly. This shows that each captures a slightly different aspect of profitability.
Leverage behaves independently. Debt-to-Equity shows a weak or negative relationship with profitability measures, echoing the AbbVie outlier effect.
Risk measures are redundant. Volatility and Beta are strongly correlated with each other (both measure market risk), so including both in a model may not add explanatory power. Total Return is also positively correlated with volatility and beta, consistent with the classic risk-return relationship.

title: Clustering
text:
Clustering is an unsupervised machine learning method. Here, instead of predicting a labeled outcome, clustering allows one to check whether the 40 companies in the dataset fall into groups based on their financial and market characteristics. Companies within a cluster should be more similar to each other than to companies in other clusters.
Partitional clustering divides the data into a fixed number of non-overlapping groups, k. The k-means clustering, for example, iteratively assigns each observation to the nearest cluster centroid and updates the centroids until they stabilize. K-means requires users to specify k in advance, and it assumes roughly spherical, similarly sized clusters.



Illustration of partitional clustering: points are assigned to a fixed number of clusters.


One the other hand, hierarchical clustering does not require one to specify k in advance. It builds a tree (dendrogram) by repeatedly merging the two closest clusters (agglomerative). One then chooses k by “cutting” the tree at a chosen height. Hierarchical clustering is more computationally expensive but reveals the full nested structure of the data.



Illustration of hierarchical clustering: a dendrogram shows nested merges of observations.


Clustering is a distance-based method, so the choice of distance metric matters. Common choices include:

Euclidean distance — straight-line distance; standard for k-means.
Manhattan distance — sum of absolute differences; more robust to outliers.
Cosine similarity/distance — measures the angle between two vectors rather than their magnitude. Useful when the shape of the feature profile matters more than its scale.
Correlation distance — like cosine but centered; captures similarity in relative patterns.

For k-means, Euclidean distance on standardized data was used, while 1 − cosine_similarity was used as the distance for hierarchical clustering.

title: Clustering
text:
K-Means: How Many Clusters?
Different values of the cluster number (k = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) are analyzed, and each was evaluated using the Average Silhouette Width (ASW). ASW ranges from −1 to 1; higher is better.


Code
library(ggplot2)

sil_df <- data.frame(
  k   = 2:6,
  asw = sapply(km_results, function(m) mean(silhouette(m$cluster, dist(X))[, 3]))
)

ggplot(sil_df, aes(x = factor(k), y = asw)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(asw, 3)), vjust = -0.5) +
  labs(x = "Number of clusters (k)", y = "Average Silhouette Width",
       title = "Silhouette Analysis: Choosing k") +
  theme_minimal()





Average Silhouette Width for k = 2 to 6




Interpretation: The ASW values are modest, which is expected since companies do not form extremely tight, well-separated clusters. The peak usually occurs around k = 3 or k = 4. Silhouette values below 0.5 indicate weak but real structure, so we treat the clusters as descriptive groupings, not hard categories.

title: Clustering
text:
Cluster Visualization
The standardized data is projected onto the first two principal components and color points by k-means cluster (k = 4).


Code
pca_res <- prcomp(X, center = FALSE, scale. = FALSE)   # X is already standardized
pca_df  <- as.data.frame(pca_res$x[, 1:2]) %>%
  mutate(cluster = factor(km_results$k4$cluster),
         ticker  = clust_ids)

ggplot(pca_df, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.8) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = ticker), size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "K-Means Clusters (k = 4) in PCA Space",
       x = "PC1", y = "PC2", color = "Cluster") +
  theme_minimal()





PCA Projection Colored by K-Means Cluster (k = 4)




Interpretation: The PCA projection shows whether clusters are visually separable in two dimensions. Tight, well-separated groups in PCA space suggest the clusters reflect genuine structure. Overlapping clusters suggest the boundaries are soft.

title: Clustering
text:
Hierarchical Clustering: Dendrogram


Code
plot(hc, labels = clust_ids, cex = 0.6, hang = -1,
     main = "Dendrogram (Cosine Distance, Average Linkage)",
     xlab = "", sub = "")
rect.hclust(hc, k = 4, border = 2:5)





Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram (Cosine Distance)




Interpretation: The dendrogram shows the full nested structure. Cutting the tree at height ~0.8–0.9 (where the largest gaps between merges occur) suggests k = 3 or k = 4, consistent with the silhouette result. Companies in the same branch share similar standardized profiles.
